Family Health

Sarcoidosis: symptoms, assessment and treatment choices

Updated: October 18, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Sarcoidosis is an inflammatory condition in which groups of immune cells form small clusters called granulomas. It often affects the lungs and lymph nodes, but can involve other organs. Some people have few symptoms and improve without medicine; others need treatment to protect organ function or improve daily life. A diagnosis does not predict one fixed course.

What sarcoidosis is and where it can occur

Granulomas can develop in the lungs, lymph nodes, skin and eyes, and sometimes the liver, spleen, heart, nervous system or other tissues. Inflammation may settle, persist or leave scarring. Which organ is involved and how well it works matter more than simply counting symptoms.

Sarcoidosis itself is not contagious and is not a form of cancer. However, infections, cancers and other inflammatory illnesses can resemble it. A symptom list or an image cannot distinguish them reliably. New symptoms deserve assessment even if sarcoidosis has already been diagnosed.

The cause is uncertain; risk patterns are not a diagnosis

The exact cause is unknown. Research suggests that immune responses to environmental or infectious triggers in susceptible people may contribute; this does not mean a specific germ, chemical or exposure has been proved to cause every case. Family history and genetic susceptibility can play a part without a simple rule that a parent passes the condition to a child.

Sarcoidosis occurs in people of different ages, sexes and ethnic backgrounds. Some populations have higher recorded rates, and childhood disease is uncommon, but being outside a commonly described group does not exclude it. Tell the clinician about family history, medicines and relevant work or environmental exposures rather than trying to diagnose it from age or ancestry.

General and breathing symptoms can vary

Some people have no symptoms and are investigated after an unrelated chest image. Others notice persistent tiredness, fever, weight loss or joint pain. Dry mouth, nasal symptoms including occasional nosebleeds, or abdominal swelling can occur but also have many other explanations. These findings do not establish sarcoidosis by themselves.

Lung involvement may cause a persistent dry cough, breathlessness, wheeze or chest discomfort. Normal-feeling breathing does not prove the lungs are unaffected. Record changes in exercise tolerance and what triggers symptoms. Do not assume new severe breathing difficulty or chest pain is an ordinary flare that can wait for a routine appointment.

Skin, eye and neurological symptoms need their own assessment

Skin changes may include tender bumps, patches, sores or changes around scars; some people develop hair loss or scarring. Enlarged lymph nodes, salivary glands, liver or spleen may also be found. Eye symptoms can include dryness, irritation, redness, pain, light sensitivity, watering or blurred vision; discharge is nonspecific and does not identify the cause. Eye inflammation can also be silent.

Nervous-system involvement can cause headache, altered sensation, facial weakness, hearing changes or seizures. Heart involvement may cause palpitations, faintness or an abnormal rhythm. These symptoms are not automatically due to sarcoidosis, and some require emergency help. Tell the team about them directly rather than mentioning only lung symptoms.

Diagnosis combines the whole picture and excludes alternatives

Assessment includes the symptom pattern, examination and medical and exposure history. A clinician may look at skin and lymph nodes, listen to the heart and lungs and check for liver or spleen enlargement. Chest X-ray or CT can show supportive patterns; lung-function tests assess breathing. Neither a spirometer result nor a chest image alone proves the diagnosis.

Sometimes a tissue sample from an appropriate site is needed to look for granulomatous inflammation, with tests to exclude causes such as infection. Biopsy is not required in every characteristic presentation, and granulomas alone are not unique to sarcoidosis. The sampling site and procedure, including bronchoscopy when appropriate, are chosen individually. Ask what each test will change and what follow-up is planned.

Check for organ involvement even when symptoms are mild

An initial assessment commonly includes an eye examination, an ECG and blood tests such as calcium, kidney function, selected liver tests and a blood count. These can reveal problems that are not obvious from symptoms. More detailed heart imaging, rhythm monitoring or neurological tests depend on the findings; not everyone needs every scan.

Keep the agreed follow-up schedule, including breathing tests or other checks when advised. Tell the team promptly about new eye, heart, nerve or urinary symptoms. Discuss calcium and vitamin D before starting supplements, because sarcoidosis can disturb calcium metabolism. Advice for bone protection, food, fluids and supplements should fit your test results and treatment, not a blanket restriction for everyone.

Treatment is available even though there is no guaranteed cure

Observation can be appropriate when symptoms are mild and organ function is not threatened, but it includes monitoring. Treatment decisions consider the organs involved, risk of damage, symptoms, quality of life and medicine harms. Corticosteroids such as prednisone are often used; other medicines, including methotrexate or selected immune-targeting drugs, may be considered by specialists.

A 2025 trial in previously untreated pulmonary sarcoidosis found methotrexate was not inferior to prednisone for the change in lung function at 24 weeks, with different side-effect patterns. That does not establish one best drug for every organ, pregnancy situation or long-term outcome. Discuss choices, necessary blood tests and infection precautions. Treatment duration varies; do not start, switch or abruptly stop prescribed steroids or other medicines on your own.

Complications depend on the organ and treatment

Persistent lung disease can cause scarring or pulmonary hypertension and impair breathing. Heart involvement can disrupt rhythm or pumping. Eye inflammation can threaten vision, and cataract or glaucoma can arise from eye disease or treatment. Nervous-system disease can affect facial or other nerves. High calcium or kidney involvement may cause stones or impaired kidney function.

Infection risk may increase with immune-suppressing treatment or damaged lungs. The team also checks treatment effects on blood counts, liver, blood sugar, blood pressure, mood and bone health as relevant. Not everyone develops these complications, and a symptom does not identify its cause. Early assessment of changes and a tailored monitoring plan are more useful than assuming either inevitable damage or universal recovery.

Daily life, fertility plans and the outlook

Many people remain active and improve over months or years, while others have relapses or a persistent condition requiring longer care. There is no promise that symptoms or treatment will end at two years. Fatigue can persist even when inflammation improves. Suitable activity, avoiding smoking and lung irritants, adequate sleep and a balanced diet can support health; they do not replace treatment when organs are at risk.

Discuss fertility or pregnancy plans early rather than assuming everyone with sarcoidosis is infertile. Organ health and medicines can affect planning; some treatments are unsuitable in pregnancy and may need a planned change before conception. Continue specialist and maternity follow-up if pregnant. Anxiety, low mood or difficulty coping also deserve care; counselling, support groups and practical help from others may be useful.

Know which changes need urgent help

Get urgent same-day advice for eye pain, marked redness, light sensitivity or new blurred vision; do not wait for the next routine eye check. New or worsening breathlessness, coughing blood, persistent or recurrent palpitations, new hearing or sensory changes, or a significant change in urine or general health should also be assessed promptly. Symptoms that have resolved after a concerning palpitation episode still need urgent advice.

Seek emergency help now for loss of vision, severe breathing difficulty, a tight or heavy chest, blue or grey colour, sudden confusion, fainting or loss of consciousness. Current palpitations with chest pain, breathlessness, dizziness or feeling faint are an emergency. Sudden facial or limb weakness, speech difficulty or sudden vision loss, and a first seizure also need emergency care. Do not drive yourself or wait to see whether these are a sarcoidosis flare.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Describe symptoms across all organ systems, bring your medicine and exposure history, and ask what the selected tests and follow-up are intended to check.

Agree monitoring or treatment with the specialist and discuss medicine risks, blood checks, supplements and pregnancy plans before changing anything yourself.

Keep eye and other follow-up appointments, but seek urgent care for new warning signs. Use emergency help for vision loss, severe breathing trouble, fainting or sudden neurological symptoms.

How BeMama can help

The practical questions are which organs are affected, whether function is changing and how symptoms affect daily life. A shared plan can combine monitoring, treatment and support without promising one timetable or assuming every symptom is caused by sarcoidosis.

When to seek help

Do not diagnose sarcoidosis from cough, a rash or one test, and do not change prescribed medicines or start calcium/vitamin D without advice. Eye pain, light sensitivity or new blurred vision needs same-day urgent assessment; new worsening breathing, blood with cough or heart/nerve changes needs prompt care. Loss of vision, severe breathing difficulty, tight/heavy chest, blue/grey colour, sudden confusion, fainting or loss of consciousness needs emergency help. Current palpitations with chest pain, breathlessness, dizziness or feeling faint, sudden face/limb weakness, speech difficulty or vision loss, and a first seizure are also emergencies. Do not drive yourself or wait for a routine review.

Evidence notes updated: October 18, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Sarcoidosis can affect several organs and may be silent; a symptom list alone cannot diagnose it.
  • The cause is uncertain and the disease is not contagious; population risk patterns are not personal predictions.
  • Diagnosis excludes alternatives and uses selected imaging, tissue sampling and organ checks.
  • Monitoring or treatment is individualized; no fixed two-year recovery or universal drug plan is guaranteed.
  • New eye, heart or nerve symptoms matter; vision loss, severe breathing problems, fainting or sudden neurological signs need emergency help.

Frequently asked questions

What causes sarcoidosis?

The precise cause is unknown. Immune responses, environmental triggers and genetic susceptibility may interact. A family history or population pattern does not mean someone will inevitably develop it. The condition itself does not spread between people.

What symptoms can occur?

There may be none, or fatigue, fever, weight loss, joint symptoms, dry cough, breathlessness or skin changes. Eyes, heart, nerves and other organs can be involved. Many symptoms have other causes, so tests and assessment are needed rather than self-diagnosis.

Is there treatment?

Yes. Some people need monitored observation; others need anti-inflammatory or immune-modifying medicines to protect organs or improve daily life. The absence of a guaranteed cure does not mean there is no effective care. Drug choice and duration depend on the individual.

What complications are possible?

Possible problems include lung scarring, heart-rhythm disturbance, eye damage, neurological disease or calcium-related kidney problems. Cataract, glaucoma and infection risk may also relate to treatment. Not everyone develops them; monitoring and timely review matter.

Can lung-function testing alone diagnose it?

No. It measures breathing performance. Diagnosis uses the clinical picture, imaging and sometimes tissue sampling, while excluding other causes. A normal test does not exclude every organ manifestation, and the appropriate tests differ between people.

Should I take calcium or vitamin D for steroid treatment?

Ask your team first. Bone protection may be important, but sarcoidosis can alter calcium metabolism and supplements need an individual plan. Do not assume everyone should take them or that everyone must avoid calcium-containing foods.

Will it disappear in two years or prevent pregnancy?

Neither is an automatic outcome. Some people improve, some have long-term disease or relapses, and fertility concerns need individual assessment. Discuss pregnancy plans and medicine safety before conception rather than stopping treatment or assuming infertility.

When should I get urgent help?

Seek same-day advice for eye pain, light sensitivity or new blurred vision and prompt assessment for worsening breathing, coughing blood or new heart/nerve symptoms. Loss of vision, severe breathing difficulty, tight/heavy chest, blue/grey colour, confusion, fainting or loss of consciousness needs emergency help. Current palpitations with chest pain, breathlessness, dizziness or faintness, sudden face or limb weakness, speech difficulty or vision loss, and a first seizure are also emergencies. Do not drive yourself.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
